newsitem.title: KENYA: Burundi defends executions, vows to act tough.
newsitem.headline: Burundi defends executions, vows to act tough.

text.p: Burundi's Foreign Minister Luc Rukingama on Friday defended last month's decision to execute six prisoners accused of genocide -- a move condemned by the U.N. Security Council.

The minister told a news conference the executions, also condemned by the European Union, the Organisation of African Unity (OAU) and neighbouring countries, was Burundi's firm attempt to end impunity in the tiny Central African nation.
Critics say the prisoners, accused of playing a leading role in 1993 inter-ethnic massacres, did not receive a fair trial before their July 31 hangings.

"We intend to see to it that criminals of genocide are fully punished. This is the start of a judicial process and we intend to strengthen the arm of our judiciary. The executions were the first signals of our commitment," Rukingama said.
He added: "We will deal firmly with criminals. We cannot allow impunity to go on unchecked."
The minister said the prisoners had received a fair trial and a court of law had found them fully reponsible for gruesome acts including the slaughter of schoolchildren.
"It was a fair trial," Rukingama said.
More than 150,000 people have died in Burundi since October 1993, when the country's first freely elected Hutu president, Melchior Ndadaye, was murdered by Tutsi troops in an attempted coup.
The coup attempt was followed by a wave of reprisals by enraged Hutus, widely regarded as "genocide" by Burundi's Tutsi minority, and counter-reprisals by the Tutsi-dominated army.
The minister accused neighbouring Tanzania, whose former president Julius Nyerere is mediating in Burundi, of siding with Hutu rebels.

Rukingama said that Tanzania had demonstrated open hostility towards Burundi by giving rebels sanctuary in the former Burundi embassy in Dar es Salaam and by spearheading regional sanctions against Bujumbura.
The minister's outbursts came 10 days ahead of the start of scheduled peace talks between Burundi's Tutsi military junta, political parties and Hutu rebels.
The talks from August 25 in the northern Tanzanian town of Arusha will be chaired by Nyerere.
"We are at a crossroads. We would like to see Tanzania take its role of mediator, we want Tanzania to facilitate the peace process and not put up hurdles to peace," Rukingama said.

He added: "We would like Tanzania to hand back to us our embassy in Dar es Salaam now occupied by rebel groups. We would like Tanzania to lift sanctions against us and adhere to international conventions."
"How can we explain to our people that Tanzania, which is mediating in Burundi, is also responsible for the sanctions against us, sanctions hurting our people?" the minister asked.

Regional countries led by Tanzania imposed sanctions on Burundi last year after Tutsi military strongman Pierre Buyoya ousted Hutu civilian president Slyvestre Ntibantunganya. But the embargo has since been eased.

Foreign ministers from neighbouring countries and Ethiopia will meet in Kampala on Saturday to review the sanctions imposed to force Buyoya to negotiate with rebels and to reintroduce constitutional rule in Burundi.
"The sanctions have had a disastrous effect on our country and we hope the meeting in Kampala will discuss the total lifting of the sanctions," Rukingama said.
He defended the policy of grouping tens of thousands of Burundians in camps, saying it was the best way of defending innocent civilians from Hutu rebels fighting the army across the country.
The U.N. World Food Programme warned on Friday that the inhabitants of the camps were not getting basic food to stave off malnutrition and life-threatening diseases.
